Key Takeaways

X-energy stock fell 23% in the past month as investors sold small-reactor stocks, Oklo and NuScale Power among them.

The company's own news was good: a joint development deal with American Electric Power and Amazon for a 960 MW plant in Indiana, and a finished NRC safety review of its Xe-100 reactor.

Wedbush initiated coverage at Buy with a $17 target, below the $31 consensus. That target is just under 9x forward sales, below the stock's average since its IPO.

Third-quarter results on Nov. 12 need to show X-energy has the cash to keep going until revenue from these projects arrives.

X-energy (XE:NASDAQ) stock is down 23% in the past month, and the other small-reactor stocks did even worse. Oklo (OKLO:NYSE) lost 35% and NuScale Power (SMR:NYSE) lost 31%, while the Nasdaq 100 fell 9%.

That's despite a month of real progress at X-energy, including a plant deal with American Electric Power (AEP:NASDAQ) and Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ). And on Nov. 2, Wedbush initiated coverage at Buy with a $17 target, 54% above the stock's current price.

Good news didn't save it

On Oct. 19, X-energy and AEP signed a joint development agreement for a proposed 12-unit, 960 MW Xe-100 plant near the former Breed coal plant in Sullivan County, Indiana. Amazon will help fund development and plans to buy the power. AEP says the plan aims to help Indiana without raising costs for its customers.

It's still feasibility work for now. But on Oct. 30, the NRC finished its final safety review of the Xe-100. That completes both of the main reviews the NRC needs before it can approve a construction permit.

Even the group's Oct. 6 rally faded. That day the reactor stocks jumped on Constellation and Google's 20-year, 890 MW nuclear power deal.

Key Takeaways

Ouster stock has dropped 34% in the past month after a hot September inflation report started a sell-off in AI and chip stocks.

Ouster's own news this month was good: a defense milestone with Forterra and a new robotics product. The drop says more about the market than about the business.

Analysts expect revenue to grow about 31% this year to $222 million, though Ouster still burns cash: $64.9 million of negative free cash flow in 2025.

Third-quarter results come Nov. 3 after the close, and the stock looks like a buy for investors who can handle big swings.

Ouster (OUST:NASDAQ) stock has dropped 34% in the past month, far more than the Nasdaq 100's 9% fall over the same stretch.

Almost all of that came from a hot inflation report and a rout in AI and chip stocks. Meanwhile, the company kept putting out good news.

Blame the inflation report

The selling picked up on Oct. 14. September's consumer price index came in at 3.7% a year, above the 3.6% economists expected and up from 3.4% in August. That raised the odds of a Federal Reserve rate hike, and AI hardware stocks took the worst of it: Nvidia, AMD and CoreWeave all fell sharply that day.

Higher rates make the AI buildout more expensive to fund, and chip stocks kept falling on Oct. 15. They slid again on Oct. 30, when Intel plunged and Amazon missed expectations.

Ouster kept winning work

On Oct. 1, just before the slide began, Ouster partnered with Seneca to put its Rev8 color lidar on Seneca's autonomous drones for wildfire response.

On Oct. 21, Ouster said Forterra's Lancer autonomous ground vehicles had completed 1,426 missions and 88 casualty evacuations in Ukraine using its sensors. A battlefield record like that should help Ouster win more defense work.

And on Oct. 27, Stereolabs, an Ouster company, launched its ZED Box 2 Series of edge AI computers for production robots.

Key Takeaways

Fiserv shares are up 17% in the past month, off their 52-week low, as payments stocks like Mastercard and Visa rallied while the Nasdaq fell.

Analysts cut their price targets through October, and Fiserv's own news didn't explain the rally.

Fiserv's third-quarter results, out today, kept its 2026 guidance in place, and the company plans to buy back $500 million of stock this quarter.

The stock trades at about 7x forward earnings, cheap enough to hold and add to, though its merchant business is still shrinking.

Fiserv (FISV:NASDAQ) stock is up 17% in the past month, off the 52-week low it hit on Oct. 2. It's still down 22% in 2026, and the company itself gave investors very little reason for the run.

Most of the lift came from money moving into payments. While the Nasdaq 100 fell 9% over the month, Mastercard rose 19% and Visa 18%.

Payments had the month tech didn't

You could see it on Oct. 22. The Nasdaq slid 3% that day, and Fiserv rose with bank-tech names Jack Henry and FIS without any news of its own.

Fiserv did have some business news. Clover passed 5 million devices shipped worldwide on Oct. 14. Five days later, Klarna said it's live at 100,000 US Clover locations and is coming to Commerce Hub, Fiserv's platform for large merchants. And on Oct. 20, Fiserv signed a multi-year deal with VikingCloud to offer cybersecurity protection to its merchants.

All good to see. But none of it explains a month like this for a $30.7 billion company.

Wall Street cut its targets the whole way up

Analysts got more cautious through October. Barclays, TD Cowen, Citi, Cantor Fitzgerald, Truist and BMO Capital all lowered their price targets, to between $48 and $53. BofA reinstated coverage with an Underperform rating and a $48 target.

Goldman Sachs was the only firm to raise its target, to $56 from $54.

So the stock rallied while most of the analysts covering it got gloomier.

UnitedHealth Just Gained 11% in a Month: Take Profits, or Buy More? ©g-stockstudio from Getty Images Pro via Canva
Key Takeaways

UnitedHealth Group (UNH) stock gained approximately 11% in the month through October 30, supported by stronger third-quarter earnings and another increase to its 2026 profit outlook.

Operating earnings climbed to $6.6 billion, while Optum Health's operating profit reached $735 million, although declining insurance membership remains a concern.

Analysts expect normalized EPS to recover to $26.99 by 2028, while shares trade at an estimated 18x forward earnings, suggesting further upside if margins continue improving.

What Happened?

UnitedHealth Group (UNH) stock gained approximately 11% between September 30 and October 30, climbing from $367 to $407, while the Nasdaq 100 declined 7% and the S&P 500 slipped 1%.

The rally followed UnitedHealth's October 13 third-quarter earnings announcement, which showed improving profitability despite continued pressure on health insurance membership.

UnitedHealth reported adjusted earnings of $4.69 per share, beating analysts' expectations of approximately $4.14. Revenue reached $112.7 billion, down slightly from $113.2 billion a year earlier.

The company also raised its full-year 2026 adjusted earnings outlook to at least $20.50 per share, marking its third guidance increase of the year.

Its medical care ratio improved to 88.4% from 89.9% a year earlier, reflecting better medical cost management and pricing discipline.

CEO Stephen Hemsley said the results reflected "the discipline and execution our teams are bringing to every part of our business."

Mizuho named UnitedHealth a top pick on October 14, while a broader rotation from technology stocks into healthcare supported managed-care companies. On October 20, RBC Capital Markets raised its price target from $478 to $498 while maintaining an Outperform rating.

Quarterly earnings from operations rose to $6.6 billion from $4.3 billion a year earlier, bringing UnitedHealth's operating margin to approximately 5.9%.

Optum Health contributed significantly to that improvement, generating $735 million in operating earnings compared with just $41 million in the prior-year quarter.

UnitedHealth's operating margin exceeded 8% annually from 2021 through 2024 before falling to 4.8% in 2025. Based on annual revenue of approximately $448 billion, every percentage point of margin recovery could represent roughly $4.5 billion in additional operating profit, assuming comparable revenue.

However, the quarter benefited from $610 million in favorable reserve development. Excluding that benefit, the medical care ratio would have been approximately 89.1%, still better than the year-earlier quarter.

US stock index futures pointed to a higher opening on Tuesday as investors looked for opportunities to buy technology shares following another sharp market decline. Nasdaq 100 futures advanced 0.8%, despite a substantial premarket drop in Apple shares, while fluctuating oil prices and stronger-than-expected US manufacturing data remained in focus.

The anticipated rebound followed a difficult Monday session in which the Nasdaq and S&P 500 reversed early gains to close at their lowest levels in three months. Concerns about the outlook for artificial intelligence continued to weigh on technology stocks, while falling crude oil prices triggered significant losses across the energy sector.

Nasdaq Futures Advance Despite Sharp Decline in Apple Shares

Nasdaq 100 futures rose 0.8% ahead of Tuesday's opening bell, suggesting renewed buying interest following the technology sector's recent selloff.

The advance came despite a 4.4% decline in premarket trading for Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL), after the iPhone manufacturer reported quarterly results that raised concerns about future profitability.

Apple recorded higher revenue and earnings but forecast a gross margin for the current quarter slightly below analyst expectations.

The company attributed the weaker-than-anticipated outlook to increasing component prices, highlighting growing cost pressures affecting its hardware business.

The announcement added to uncertainty surrounding technology shares, which have already faced significant selling pressure in recent sessions.

Nevertheless, the positive movement in Nasdaq futures suggested that some investors were seeking buying opportunities following the market's recent declines.

Nasdaq and S&P 500 Close at Three-Month Lows

Wall Street experienced a volatile trading session on Monday, with major indices initially advancing before reversing direction.

The Nasdaq Composite fell 272.68 points, or 1.1%, to close at 25,164.32.

The S&P 500 declined 38.67 points, or 0.5%, to finish at 7,541.40.

Both indices extended the losses recorded during the previous Thursday and Friday sessions, reaching their lowest closing levels in three months.

The reversal reflected continued weakness in technology shares and renewed concerns about the outlook for artificial intelligence-related investments.

Although bargain hunting initially supported the market, selling pressure intensified as the session progressed, erasing early gains.

Dow Jones Advances as Consumer and Industrial Stocks Gain

Unlike the Nasdaq and S&P 500, the Dow Jones Industrial Average managed to finish Monday's session in positive territory.
